0: Author: Bao Qiming, AI Research Scientist&Engineer @Xtracta, ModelScope community contributor
2: "AI Scientist" is a hot topic in the Agent space recently: let large models propose hypotheses, design experiments, analyze data, and finally draw conclusions on their own. But if you directly let models do open-ended scientific research, you quickly run into two problems: first, small models struggle to complete it; second, the results cannot be judged right or wrong—the model says "I discovered X", but there is no standard answer to check against, so there is no way to compare the quality of different models and different Agent designs.
3: We take a different approach: first compress scientific research into a minimal but complete closed loop that can be automatically verified. The research object is a "black-box machine" that takes two integers a and b (0–20) as input and outputs an integer; the internal rule is unknown and may include conditional branches, for example "when a is even, output a+b; otherwise output a×b". The model can only learn about it by running experiments, and finally submits a rule. Because there are only 21×21=441 possible inputs, the submitted rule can be checked one by one on all inputs, without needing an LLM as a judge.
4: This article uses the Qwen3 series open-source models and vLLM to build this Mini AI Scientist step by step in a ModelScope Notebook, and answers a practical question: how small can an open-source model be to complete this kind of "scientific discovery"? Is the bottleneck model scale, thinking mode, or the Agent's workflow design?
8: Give an open-source model a black-box machine with a hidden rule, let it propose hypotheses, design experiments, call Python to test and revise on its own, and finally submit a rule, which the program exhaustively verifies as right or wrong on 441 inputs.
10: Developers working on LLM Agents, reasoning, and evaluation; those who want to apply AI Scientist to quantifiable experiments; trainers who need verifiable reward environments (such as GRPO).

17: The inputs, outputs, and completion boundaries of this Case are as follows:
20: A black-box machine with hidden rules (12 rules, 3 difficulty levels), an experiment budget of 30, and a maximum of 15 rounds of interaction
22: The rules submitted by the model (Python expressions), the complete research process record (JSONL), and the automatic evaluation results (whether correct, consistency rate, number of experiments)
24: The submitted rules must be fully consistent with the true rules on all 441 inputs to count as a "successful discovery"
26: The rules are deterministic functions on two integer inputs, involving no noise, continuous variables, or real physical experiments (see Section 7 for extension directions)
28: The overall approach is to let the model and Python each play their own role: the model is responsible for decisions (what hypotheses to propose, what experiments to run, when to draw conclusions), Python is responsible for execution and verification (running experiments, computing, and checking hypotheses one by one), and the black-box laboratory holds the ground truth (the final exhaustive verification). 29: In each round, the model outputs a JSON action, choosing one of the following four tools:
34: Select up to 6 sets of inputs and run them on the black-box machine
37: Have Python compute derived columns over all observations, e.g. out - a*b, and indicate which column is constant
40: Use candidate rules to check the observed data one by one, and list the correct and incorrect rows
42: Submit the final rule and end the research
44: Around these four tools, the code is divided into several modules:
47: Store 12 real rules; run experiments; perform equivalence verification on 441 inputs
49: Only arithmetic, comparison, X if C else Y, and abs/min/max are allowed; arbitrary code execution is rejected
51: Parse actions, call tools, organize feedback; use an "experiment notebook" to store verified hypotheses, keep only the most recent 3 rounds of dialogue, and control context length
53: At submission, if the rules contradict data the model itself has observed, reject and list the contradicting rows
55: Use vLLM for batch inference; strip the <think> reasoning content and write only the final action back to the dialogue
56: There are three considerations in the selection. First, the Qwen3 series covers 0.6B–8B within the same family and can toggle thinking mode per request, making it suitable for a "scale × thinking" comparison. Second, vLLM: thinking mode generates thousands of tokens per round; running Qwen3-8B with transformers takes 28 minutes for 4 episodes, whereas switching to vLLM batch inference takes only 33 minutes for 36 episodes. Third, exhaustive verification rather than an LLM judge: the input space has only 441 cases, equivalence can be determined exactly, and evaluation is zero-cost and unambiguous.

85: We first verify the modules that do not depend on the model (4.1–4.3, CPU is sufficient), and then connect the model (4.4–4.8). At the end of each step there is a check cell that uses assert to determine whether the step succeeded.
87: Goal: construct the research subject—a black-box machine whose rules are unknown but whose ground truth can be exhaustively verified.
88: Inputs and operations: 12 rules across three difficulty levels. Tier 1 is a single formula (such as a + b); Tier 2 has one conditional branch (such as switching formulas based on the parity of a); Tier 3 is nested conditions or modulo conditions (such as (a + b) % 5 == 0). Lab(rule, seed) uses a random seed to generate 3 initial observations.
89: Check method: each true rule must be 100% correct when validated against itself; the initial observations for the same seed must be exactly the same.
90: 4.2 A safe sandbox that lets the model "call Python"
91: Goal: the rules and calculation expressions written by the model must actually be executed, but arbitrary code must not be executed.
92: Inputs and operations: compile_expr first parses the expression's syntax tree and only allows arithmetic, comparisons, X if C else Y, and abs/min/max; exponents are only allowed to be constants from 0 to 4.
93: Check method: __import__, attribute access, and oversized exponents must be rejected; the judgment is based on semantic equivalence, so max(a, b) - min(a, b) should also be judged as the correct answer for |a - b|.
94: 4.3 Dry-run the Agent loop with a "scripted model"
95: Goal: before connecting the real model, first confirm that the Agent loop, the four tools, and the evaluation process themselves have no problems.
96: Input and operation: Walk through it once with a fake model that replies according to a fixed script: run experiment → compute → test wrong hypothesis → test correct hypothesis → submit. The notebook also prints the system prompt that the model actually sees.
97: Check method: The dry run must "find success", with 3 experiments, 2 tests, 1 computation, and no format errors. In the figure below you can see the check feedback: for the wrong hypothesis a - b, the correct and incorrect rows are listed, helping the model locate the conditional branch.
99: Goal: Load Qwen3-4B on the GPU with thinking mode enabled.
101: Meaning of a few key parameters: max_tokens=8192 is the upper limit for thinking plus answer per turn; max_model_len=20480 is the context length, and since the lab notebook keeps conversations very short, this length is sufficient; sampling uses the thinking-mode parameters officially recommended for Qwen3, temperature=0.6, top_p=0.95, top_k=20, because greedy decoding easily traps thinking models in loops; gpu_memory_utilization=0.85 allows 4B to run normally on a 24GB GPU, and if VRAM is insufficient you can lower it or switch to Qwen/Qwen3-1.7B.

105: Goal: Observe how the model starts from 3 initial observations, runs experiments and tests step by step, until it submits.
106: Input and operation: Rule parity_a (Tier 2: output a + b when a is even, otherwise output a * b), with initial seed 0. The model cannot see the true rule.
107: Process and output: The figure below is a real run. From the 3 initial observations the model guesses "switch by the parity of a", then verifies it with two controlled experiments (2,3) and (3,4), and submits after confirmation; all 441 inputs are consistent, taking 76 seconds.
108: Check method: The process finishes completely and yields a verification result. Because sampling is stochastic, a single run may succeed or fail, which is exactly why Section 4.6 uses multiple rules for statistics.
110: Goal: Measure the Agent's discovery ability under a unified protocol.
111: Input and operation: Create one episode for each of the 12 rules (seed 0), advance all episodes synchronously, and perform one batch inference per round:

114: 4.7 Analyzing failures: the model "contradicts" its own data
115: Goal: Determine whether the failures are really "failing to find the pattern" or something else.
116: Input and operation: For each failed episode, check the rule submitted by the model line by line against all the experiments it ran itself.
117: Process and output: In this run, 1 of the 6 failures submitted a rule that contradicted its own data (threshold_b, 2 contradictory rows), and another 1 (nested) never submitted at all. This proportion varies greatly across configurations: in the full experiment, Qwen3-8B without thinking had 23/24 failures of this kind, which dropped to 10/20 with thinking enabled (see Section 5). In other words, many failures are not due to inability to discover, but to drawing conclusions without checking.
118: Check method: In the table, "number of rows contradicting its own data" of 0 means the rule is consistent with existing data but still wrong (data insufficient to rule it out), greater than 0 means self-contradictory, and -1 means not submitted.
120: Goal: Write the research norm "conclusions must be consistent with one's own data" into the Agent.
121: Input and operation: Episode(..., gate=True), with all other settings identical to 4.6. At submission, if the rule contradicts observed data, the submission is rejected, the contradictory rows are listed, and the model is told to continue researching. To ensure every episode can end, the submission in the final round bypasses the gate.
122: Process and output: Measured runtime was 1007 seconds, the number solved changed from 6/12 to 7/12, and the gate intercepted 5 contradictory submissions in total.
123: Check method: A rejected count greater than 0 indicates that the gate did indeed intercept contradictory conclusions. Single-seed differences are subject to randomness; see Section 5 for multi-seed, multi-scale results.

128: 5.1 Thinking mode matters more than parameter count
131: Contradicts its own data in failures (off → on)
148: After enabling thinking at each scale, the solve rate improves noticeably; the 1.7B with thinking enabled (14/36) already surpasses the 8B without thinking (12/36). The gap between 4B and 8B (with thinking) is within random fluctuation, so for this task, 4B is already sufficient, and it can also run on ModelScope's free GPU.
149: The last column of the table reveals the main benefit brought by thinking: without thinking, failures are almost all "submitted rules that contradict one's own experimental data"; with thinking enabled, such failures drop significantly (with the exception of 0.6B, which still mostly contradicts itself even with thinking enabled).
150: 5.2 Submission gate: it can block contradictory conclusions, but whether it can correct them depends on the model
165: The checkpoint can only tell the model "your conclusion contradicts the data," not how to fix it. Models with thinking on are sometimes able to self-correct after being stopped, hence the slight improvement; the 8B with thinking off repeatedly submits wrong rules after being stopped until it runs out of turns. These differences are all within random fluctuation. Our conclusion is: process design can help models avoid jumping to conclusions, but the ability to revise hypotheses still depends on the model's own reasoning.
170: Only 0.36 compute calls per episode on average
175: compute was originally designed for models that don't think and are prone to mental arithmetic errors. Models with thinking on compute on their own during the thinking process and barely use this tool (1.7B uses only 0.06 calls per episode on average), and removing it causes no degradation. Assistance necessary for weak models may just be a redundant option for strong models.
177: The previous generation of non-reasoning models is clearly weaker: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and 3B-Instruct both score 5/36, 1.5B scores 0/36, and there is no improvement from 3B to 7B.
178: Tier 3 remains the capability boundary: for rules with nested or modulo conditions, the best result across all configurations is only 2/12 (Qwen3-8B with thinking enabled + submission checkpoint).

185: We use three metrics: discovery success rate (the proportion of submitted rules that exactly match the true rule on all 441 inputs, reported stratified by difficulty), agreement rate (the proportion of inputs on which the submitted rule and the true rule produce the same result, used to measure partial correctness), and experiment efficiency (the average number of experiments used when successful). For Qwen3-4B with thinking enabled, the normal range for a single seed is overall ≥4/12 and Tier 1 ≥3/4.
186: As a control, we also implemented a baseline that does not use an LLM: it performs experiments randomly while excluding candidates inconsistent with the data from about 12,000 candidate rules of the form F if C else G.
187: The exhaustive baseline solves 32/36, which appears better than the LLM, but it has two fundamental limitations: first, its expressive power is limited by the candidate grammar, and two-level nested rules are not in the candidate space and can never be discovered; second, its experiments are blind, and even for the simplest Tier 1 rules it requires an average of 29 experiments, whereas Qwen3-8B and 4B with thinking enabled, when successful, used only 3.9 and 7.6 experiments on average. The value of the LLM scientist lies in designing experiments in a targeted way; the gap lies in the reliability of reasoning.

207: 7. Known limitations, troubleshooting, and reusable directions
209: The rule space is small (two integer inputs, deterministic output), so there is still a gap from real scientific research.
210: Sampling is stochastic, so single runs fluctuate; conclusions should be based on multi-seed statistics. Each configuration in this paper has only 36 episodes, so small differences are not statistically significant.
211: Tier 3 rules remain difficult for models up to 8B.
212: Thinking mode costs about 10–14 times the compute of non-thinking mode, and about 10%–20% of turns are truncated because the thinking is too long.

235: The structure of "model decision + Python execution + ground-truth verification" is also applicable to scenarios such as automated evaluation of data analysis Agents, SQL and formula inference, system identification, and fault localization.

264: This article uses open-source models to build a Mini AI Scientist that can be automatically verified: the model is responsible for proposing hypotheses, designing experiments, and drawing conclusions, while Python handles execution and validation, and exhaustive verification gives definitive right or wrong answers. Experiments show that on this task, a 4B model with thinking enabled can already precisely discover more than half of the hidden rules; the main role of thinking mode is to keep the model's conclusions consistent with its own experimental data. The low success rate on Tier 3 rules also reminds us that small models are still a considerable distance from reliable "scientific discovery"—this verifiable environment can serve precisely as a starting point for subsequent improvements and training.
